analysis.investment_thesis: Balu Forge is a genuinely excellent business — ROCE of 31.3% and operating margins of 26% confirm a high-quality industrial compounder — but at an earnings yield of only ~4.3% (EBIT INR 251 Cr / EV ~INR 5,850 Cr), it fails the Magic Formula's cheapness test by a wide margin. Wait for the price to come to you; quality alone is not sufficient at any price.
key_strengths: ROCE of 31.3% is well above the 25% Magic Formula excellence threshold — rare in capital-heavy manufacturing
Operating margins expanded from ~9% (2021) to 26% (2025) with revenue CAGR of 60% — genuine operating leverage at scale
Near-zero leverage (D/E 0.07) with reserves jumping from INR 9 Cr to INR 1,135 Cr — pristine balance sheet self-funded by equity raises
key_risks: Earnings yield ~4.3% (EBIT/EV) is well below the 6% floor — the stock is materially overvalued by Magic Formula standards
Free cash flow was negative INR 268 Cr in FY25 and negative INR 166 Cr in FY24 — accounting profits massively exceed cash generation; capex INR 416 Cr vs. net profit INR 204 Cr
CWIP of INR 351 Cr (23% of total assets) signals heavy capacity build-out — execution risk is high and returns on this new capital are unproven
red_flags: FCF negative 3 of last 4 years — capital-consumption business disguised as a compounder
Operating CF was negative in FY22 (−58 Cr) and FY24 (−32 Cr) — working capital absorbs cash during growth spurts
EV/EBITDA of 17.5x on a manufacturing business with unproven new capacity; Magic Formula would demand sub-10x for a buy signal
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Running the Magic Formula: EBIT (Operating Income) of INR 251 Cr against an Enterprise Value of roughly INR 5,850 Cr (market cap INR 5,903 Cr + debt INR 40 Cr − cash INR 93 Cr) yields an earnings yield of only 4.3%. That is below the 6% floor where the formula even begins to get interested, and far below the 12–15% range that signals a genuine bargain. On the other side, ROCE of 31.3% is excellent and the business clearly earns well above its cost of capital on deployed assets. But the Magic Formula requires BOTH metrics to rank well — one out of two is not enough to act.

The deeper concern from a Greenblatt lens is cash quality. Net profit of INR 204 Cr in FY25 looks terrific, but FCF was negative INR 268 Cr because capex hit INR 416 Cr. That capex is flowing into CWIP of INR 351 Cr — capacity that has not yet earned a rupee. If this capacity comes online and sustains 30%+ ROIC, the investment case improves materially as EBIT scales into the existing enterprise value. Until then, the Magic Formula cannot endorse paying 17.5x EBITDA for earnings that are not yet converting to cash. Watch the stock; revisit when CWIP converts to productive assets and earnings yield moves above 8%.
